stances.claim: The SC's voiding of the JMSU is 'a subtle reminder' to Philippine negotiators to comply rigorously with the two constitutional safeguards on EDU of natural resources -- full state control and 60% Filipino capital -- which are 'sacred' and must be strictly observed.
stances.rhetorical_move: constitutional-safeguard insistence dressed as a reminder

stances.claim: The Court properly went beyond the literal label 'pre-exploration activities' and looked at the parties' intent -- discovering petroleum is 'tantamount to exploration,' regardless of how it is dressed in the contract.

The February 2022 MOU provision making oil-and-gas operations 'subject to the laws of the Philippines' (without prejudice to either party's SCS claims) satisfies the constitutional safeguards on 'full control' and 'citizenship.'
stances.rhetorical_move: respectful constitutional certification of the draft MOU

stances.claim: Now that the Chinese panel has been made aware of the safeguards and of the limits on the Philippine panel's authority, China should agree to finalize the draft MOU; a refusal would signal that China is not really interested.

If China continues to procrastinate, the President may permissibly abandon government-to-government talks and pivot to the United States -- opening a path for 24/7 US deployment in the EEZ under the Mutual Defense Treaty, including treating an attack on a Coast Guard vessel as an attack on the Philippines.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban reads the Supreme Court's 12-2-1 decision (penned by Justice Samuel H. Gaerlan) voiding the Tripartite JMSU among China's CNOOC, Vietnam Oil and Gas Corporation, and the Philippine National Oil Company as 'a subtle reminder' to Philippine negotiators to comply rigorously with two 'sacred' constitutional safeguards on the exploration, development, and utilization of natural resources: full state control and supervision, and the 60% Filipino-capital requirement. He praises the Court for going beyond the literal label 'pre-exploration activities' and looking at the parties' intent -- discovering petroleum is 'tantamount to exploration,' regardless of how it is dressed. He then aims the message simultaneously at both negotiating panels in the EEZ Joint Development MOU talks. The Philippine panel is reminded how far it may give in to Chinese demands; the Chinese panel is told that the Philippine panel is powerless to go beyond the February 2022 draft MOU, which makes oil-and-gas operations 'subject to the laws of the Philippines' without prejudice to either party's SCS claims -- a provision CJ respectfully submits already satisfies the constitutional safeguards. If China nonetheless wants to restart from scratch, that 'procrastination smacks of just dribbling the ball and refusing to take a shot' -- a wasteful tactic 'rejected in basketball-crazy Philippines.' He would not fault the President for reverting to his late-November 2022 stance that the country may abandon government-to-government talks and 'find other ways,' which could include turning to the United States under the PH-US Mutual Defense Treaty -- a pivot that could permit 24/7 US deployment in the EEZ and arguably treat an attack on a Philippine Coast Guard vessel as an attack on the Philippines. He inserts an aside from Eddie Yap (Edsa Busway advocate) on why a lay-clear constitutional question took 15 years to decide, promising a fuller answer later. The column closes with condolences to the late Ambassador Manuel M. Lopez.
